title: Audit log compression and query-cost PRD (sketch)
content:
Purpose
This document sketches a PRD for reducing audit log egress and storage cost in Private deployments by applying compression, tiered retention, and query-cost-aware indexes while preserving forensic utility and approval-gate traceability. Focus is customer-managed networking and air-gapped/on-prem installs where bandwidth and storage economics vary significantly.

Problem statement
Customers running Redwood Private in constrained datacenters or across costly egress links have asked for: (1) lower storage and transfer costs for audit artifacts; (2) fast, cheap queries for common troubleshooting scenarios; (3) ability to produce compact, verifiable evidence for audits and approvals without shipping full raw logs every time. Current model: full uncompressed events + optional sampling. This leads to spikes in S3 usage, slow forensic runs, and friction in approval flows when evidence must be zipped and couriered.

Goals
- Reduce long-term audit storage cost by ~50% for standard workloads through compression + index strategies.
- Provide query latency SLOs for common filters (time range + approval-id + user-id) under 2s for small time windows (<= 1 hour) and <15s for 30d window on typical Dedicated nodes.
- Maintain cryptographic verifiability of compressed artifacts (hash chains / signed manifests) so compressed stores remain admissible for audits.
- Expose a low-cost "evidence snapshot" API that returns minimal proof bundles for approval gates (summary + required deltas) rather than entire logs.
- Keep UX simple: default safe config for most customers, opt-in aggressive tiers for customers who accept longer forensic restores.

Non-goals
- Replace full-fidelity raw logging for customers that explicitly require uncompressed retention for regulatory reasons.
- Re-architect existing approval gate semantics; this focuses on storage & retrieval layers.

Design ideas (sketch)
1) Tiered storage with per-tenant policies
- Hot tier (0-7d): raw or lightly compressed events, fast indexes, retained on local SSD/NVMe. Used for live troubleshooting and approval rollbacks.
- Warm tier (8-90d): block-compressed event bundles (e.g., Zstd level 9) with lightweight per-bundle indexes (min/max timestamp, approval-ids, user-ids, event-types). Bundles stored in cheaper object store (customer-managed blob).
- Cold tier (90+d): columnar compressed archives (e.g., Parquet with Zstd) optimized for long-range analytics and compliance exports; retrieval may involve a restore process (minutes to hours).

2) Bundle layout and indexing
- Events are batched into time-window bundles (default 5m / 50k events) and compressed. Each bundle contains an index file: list of keys (approval-id, request-id, tenant-id, hashed-subject, timestamps) and per-key offsets.
- Index entries are kept small (utf8 keys, 8-byte offsets) and optionally replicated in a separate compact index DB for fast point lookups.
- Offer two index modes: "embedded" (indexes within bundle for easy shipping) and "sidecar" (high-performance DB like RocksDB for on-prem hot tier). Sidecar is default in Dedicated nodes.

3) Evidence snapshot API and proof manifests
- Snapshot API: GET /v1/private/{tenant}/evidence?snapshot=approval-id&window=... returns: compact summary (counts, sample events), signed manifest (bundle ids + offsets), and compressed digests required to prove continuity.
- Manifest format: list of bundle-ids + SHA256 per-bundle + offset ranges. Server signs manifest with customer or Redwood key depending on deployment model.
- Restore operation can stream only the necessary bundles/offsets for an approval, avoiding full-log transfer.

4) Query-cost-aware execution
- Queries targeting small key-value filters (approval-id, request-id) use sidecar index to locate offsets and stream only matching event slices. Cost estimate returned to caller before heavy reads (byte estimate + ETA).
- For large range queries, run a two-phase plan: (a) index scan to enumerate bundles, (b) parallel fetch + decompress with rate limits. UI surfaces cost/latency tradeoff and optional throttling.

5) On-customer pre-aggregation to reduce egress
- For VPC/private installs, provide an optional lightweight aggregator that computes per-approval summaries and cryptographic commitments locally, synced to Redwood control plane. This reduces the need to fetch raw logs for routine approval validation.

Security & compliance
- All compressed bundles are encrypted at rest using customer KMS where available.
- Manifests are signed and support key rotation. Must support local HSM/KMS in Private deployments.
- Chain-of-custody: each bundle contains a monotonic sequence number and previous-bundle-hash to detect tampering.

UX considerations / Console flows
- Default retention slider per-tenant with recommended presets: "Balanced" (7/60/365), "Cost-Optimized" (1/30/365+cold), "Forensic-Ready" (14/180/730).
- When an approval gate requests evidence, Console shows an "evidence cost" modal with estimated bytes and time and a one-click "compact proof" option that returns the signed manifest + top-10 sample events.
- CLI tool to fetch expand bundles for offline forensic analysis with progress and resume.

Acceptance criteria (MVP)
- Hot/warm/cold tiers implemented with basic bundle + embedded index format.
- Snapshot API returns signed manifests and streams required offsets.
- Sidecar index option available and improves point queries by >=5x vs full scan.
- Retention presets + Console UX for showing cost estimates.
- End-to-end test: generate simulated approval workflow with 1M events; verify evidence snapshot for a single approval returns <=500KB manifest and required events within ETA.

Metrics to track
- Median bytes stored per tenant/day (baseline vs post-change).
- % of approval evidence requests satisfied without moving to cold restore.
- Query latencies for typical lookups (1hr window) and cost estimate accuracy (estimated vs actual bytes).
- Restore failure rate and time-to-first-byte.

Operational concerns and risks
- Complexity of bundle indexes and state management across upgrades. Mitigation: schema versioning + migration plan and feature flag.
- Regulatory customers that require plaintext logs in-place—need opt-out and documented tradeoffs.
- Edge-case: when an approval references events crossing bundle boundaries; ensure snapshot API composes multi-bundle offsets efficiently.
- Cost: added CPU for compression on write. Mitigation: tunable compression levels and background compaction.

Open questions / research tasks
- What compression codec best balances speed and ratio for our event schema? (Zstd vs LZ4 vs Brotli). Run benchmarks on sample corpora.
- Should manifests be signed with customer key by default in VPC mode? (Legal implications).
- How large should the default bundle window be for low-latency queries vs best compression? (tunable)
- Sidecar index storage: RocksDB on NVMe is cheap but adds ops burden. Offer as opt-in for heavy customers.

Next steps / roadmap (rough)
- Week 0-4: Benchmark compression codecs + bundle window experiments (eng: Infra + Applied ML).
- Week 4-8: Implement bundle format + embedded index + basic compression in Private deploy artifact.
- Week 8-12: Sidecar index prototype + Snapshot API + Console modal for evidence cost.
- Week 12-16: End-to-end tests, encryption/KMS integration, docs, and beta with 2 customer pilots.

Notes to self
- Coordinate with legal on manifest signature language and admissibility.
- Sync with Solutions Eng on CLI UX needs for offline compliance teams.
- Rack up sample corpora from customer pilot (anonymized) for compression experiments.

References and inspiration
- Internal: audit-telemetry-consolidation (Confluence) and PD-8421 ticket.
- External: Parquet/Zstd best practices; forensic chain-of-custody whitepapers.
